source_text: Haec Platonici, subtilitate potius quam veritate, conturbant. Omne, inquiunt, corpus, aut animale sit necesse est, aut inanimale. Et siquidem inanimale est, extrinsecus movebitur; si vero animale, intrinsecus. Anima autem nec intrinsecus movebitur, ut quae non sit inanimalis; nec extrinsecus, ut quae ipsa potius moveat corpus. Itaque non videri eam corpus, quae non corporalium fornia ex aliqua regione moveatur. Ad hoc nos mirabimur incongruentiam primo definitionis provocantis ad ea quae in animam non conveniunt. Non enim potest anima animale corpus dici, aut inanimale; cum ipsa sit quae aut faciat corpus animale, si adsit; aut inanimale, si absit ab illo. Itaque quod facit, non potest esse ipsa, ut dicatur animale vel inanimale. Anima enim dicitur substantiae suae nomine. Quod si non capit animale corpus dici aut inanimale quod est anima, quomodo provocabitur ad animalium et inanimalium corporum formam? Dehinc, si corporis est moveri extrinsecus ab aliquo; ostendimus autem supra moveri animam et ab alio cum vaticinatur, cum furit, utique extrinsecus, cum ab alio: merito quod movebitur extrinsecus ab alio, secundum exempli propositionem, corpus agnoscam. Enim vero, si ab alio moveri corporis est, quanto magis movere aliud? Anima autem movet corpus, et conatus ejus extrinsecus, foris parent. Ab illa est enim impingi et pedes in incessum, et manus in contactum, et oculos in conspectum, et linguam in effatum, velut sigillario motu superficiem intus agitante. Unde haec vis incorporal animae? unde vacuae rei solida propellere? Sed quomodo divisi videntur in homine sensus corporales et intellectuales? Corporalium aiunt rerum ualitates, ut terrae, ut ignis, corporalibus sensibus renuntiari, ut tactu, ut visu: incorporalium vero intellectualibus conveniri, ut benignitatis, vel malignitatis. Itaque incorporalem esse animam constat, cujus qualitates non corporalibus, sed intellectualibus sensibus comprehendantur. Plane, si non hujus definitionis gradum exclusero. Ecce enim, incorporalia ostendo corporalibus sensibus subjici, sonum auditui, colorem conspectui, odorem odoratui: quorum exemplo etiam anima corpori accedit, ne dicas idcirco ea per corporales renuntiari sensus, quia corporalibus accedant. Igitur si constat incorporalia quoque a corporalibus comprehendi, cur non et anima, quae corporalis, ab incorporalibus renuntietur? Certe definitio exclusa sit. De insignioribus argumentationibus erit etiam illa, quod omne corpus corporalibus ali judicant; animam vero ut incorporalem, incorporalibus, sapientiae scilicet studiis. Sed nec hic gradus stabit, etiam Sorano methodicae medicinae instructissimo auctore respondente animam corporalibus quoque ali; denique, deficientem eam cibo plerumque fulciri. Quidni, quo adempto, in totum dilabitur ex corpore? Ita etiam ipse Soranus plenissime super anima commentatus quatuor voluminibus, et cum omnibus philosophorum sententiis expertus, corporalem animae substantiam vindicat, etsi illam immortalitate fraudavit. Non enim omnium est credere, quod Christianorum est. Sicut ergo Soranus ipse rebus ostendit animam corporalibus ali, proinde et philosophus exhibeat illam incorporalibus pasci. Sed nemo unquam cunctanti de exitu animae mulsam aquam de eloquio Platonis infudit; aut micas de minutiloquio Aristotelis infersit. Quid autem facient tot ac tantae animae rupicum et barbarorum, quibus alimenta sapientiae desunt, tamen indoctae prudentia pollent, et sine academiis et porticibus atticis, et carceribus Socratis, denique jejunantes philosophia, nihilominus vivunt. Non enim substantiae ipsi alimenta proficiunt studiorum, sed disciplinae; quia nec opimiorem animam efficiunt, sed ornatiorem. Bene autem, quod et artes Stoici corporales adfirmant. Adeo sic quoque anima corporalis, si et artibus ali creditur. Sed enormis intentio philosophiae solet plerumque nec prospicere pro pedibus: sic Thales in puteum. Solet et, sententias non intelligendo, valetudinis corruptelam suspicari: sic Chrysippus ad elleborum. Tale aliquid, opinor, ei accidit, cum duo in unum corpora negavit, alienatus a prospectu et recogitatu praegnantum, quae non singula quotidie corpora, sed et bina et terna in unius uteri ambitu perferunt. Invenitur etiam in jure civili graeca quaedam quinionem enixa filiorum, semel omnium mater, unici foetus parens multiplex, unici uteri puerpera numerosa, quae tot stipata corporibus, pene dixerim populo, sextum ipsa corpus fuit. Universa conditio testabitur, corpora de corporibus processura jam illic esse, unde procedunt: secundum sit necesse est, quod ex alio est: nihil porro ex alio est, nisi dum gignitur: sed tunc duo sunt.
thought_title: Refutation of Platonic Ideas on the Soul
pass_a_gloss: These things the Platonists confuse with subtlety rather than truth. They say that every body is necessarily either animate or inanimate. And indeed if it is inanimate, it will be moved from outside; if truly animate, from within. But the soul will be moved neither from within, as if it were not inanimate; nor from outside, as if it itself rather moves the body. Therefore, it does not seem to be a body, which is not moved by the forms of corporeal things from some region. We marvel at this inconsistency, first, of a definition that provokes those things which do not apply to the soul. For the soul cannot be called an animate body or an inanimate body; since it itself is that which makes the body animate, if it is present; or inanimate, if it is absent from it. Therefore, what it does, it cannot be itself, so that it may be called animate or inanimate. For the soul is called by the name of its substance. But if the soul, which is not a body, cannot be called animate or inanimate, how will it be provoked to the form of animate and inanimate bodies? Next, if it is a property of a body to be moved from outside by something; and we show above that the soul is moved by another, both when it prophesies and when it is mad, certainly from outside, by another: rightly, therefore, what is moved from outside by another, according to the proposition of the example, I recognize as a body. For if it is a property of a body to be moved by another, how much more to move another? But the soul moves the body, and its efforts are evident from outside, from without. For it is from the soul that the feet are impelled to walk, and the hands to touch, and the eyes to see, and the tongue to speak, just as a seal impresses a surface with a motion that stirs from within. Whence is this power of the incorporal soul? Whence does a vacant thing propel solid things? But how do the senses seem to be divided in man into corporeal and intellectual? They say that the powers of corporeal things, such as earth and fire, are announced by corporeal senses, such as touch and sight: but the incorporal things are suited to intellectual senses, such as kindness and malice. Therefore, it is agreed that the soul is incorporal, whose qualities are comprehended not by corporeal senses, but by intellectual senses. Clearly, if I have not excluded the step of this definition. For behold, I show that incorporal things are subject to corporeal senses, sound to hearing, color to sight, odor to smell: by whose example the soul also approaches the body, lest you say that it is announced by corporeal senses for this reason, because it approaches corporeal things. Therefore, if it is agreed that incorporal things are also comprehended by corporeal things, why not also the soul, which is corporeal, announced by incorporal things? Certainly, the definition is excluded. Of the more notable arguments, there will also be that which says that every body is judged by corporeal things; but the soul, as incorporal, by incorporal things, namely, the studies of wisdom. But neither will this step stand, since even Soranus, the most instructed author of methodical medicine, responding that the soul is also nourished by corporeal things; and finally, that it is often supported when it is deficient in food. Why not, since when it is taken away, it slips away entirely from the body? Thus, even Soranus himself, who has commented most fully on the soul in four volumes, and has experienced all the opinions of the philosophers, vindicates the corporeal substance of the soul, although he has deprived it of immortality. For it is not for all to believe what is of the Christians. Just as, therefore, Soranus himself shows that the soul is nourished by corporeal things, so also let the philosopher show that it is fed by incorporal things. But no one has ever poured sweet water into the discourse of Plato, or sprinkled dust from the minutiae of Aristotle. What, then, will so many and such great souls of rustics and barbarians do, who lack the nourishment of wisdom, yet are powerful in untaught prudence, and without academies and Attic porticos, and the prisons of Socrates, finally, fasting from philosophy, nonetheless live? For it is not the nourishment of substances that profits the studies, but the disciplines; because they do not make the soul more rich, but more ornate. But, indeed, the Stoics also affirm that the arts are corporeal. So, therefore, the soul is also corporeal, if it is believed to be nourished by the arts. But the enormous intention of philosophy usually does not look ahead, even to its feet: thus Thales into a well. It usually also suspects a corruption of health, not understanding the opinions: thus Chrysippus to the hellebore. Something of this kind, I think, happened to it, when it denied that two bodies can be in one, having lost sight of and recollection of pregnant women, who do not daily carry single bodies, but also two and three in the compass of one womb. It is also found in civil law that a certain Greek woman gave birth to five children, once the mother of all, the parent of a single fetus, the mother of many children, who, packed with so many bodies, was, I would say, a people, was herself the sixth body. The whole condition will testify that bodies proceed from bodies, even from that place from which they proceed: it is necessary that what is from another is second; nothing, moreover, is from another, unless it is being born: but then there are two.
pass_b_english: The Platonists muddle these matters with cleverness rather than truth. They insist every body must be either animate or inanimate. If it's inanimate, it gets moved from outside; if animate, from within. But the soul fits neither: it isn't moved from within, since it's not inanimate, nor from outside, since it's the very thing that moves the body. So it doesn't look like a body at all—one that isn't shifted by corporeal forms from some quarter. We're left gaping at the first incoherence: a definition that drags in categories that simply don't apply to the soul. The soul can't be called an animate body or an inanimate one, because it's the cause: it makes a body animate when present, inanimate when absent. What produces a condition can't itself be that condition. The soul bears the name of its own substance. If something that isn't a body can't be labeled animate or inanimate, how can it be forced into the mold of animate and inanimate bodies?

Next: if being moved from outside by something else is a mark of a body, then we've already shown the soul is moved by another—when it prophesies, when it raves—certainly from outside, by another. So by the very logic of the example, I'd have to call the soul a body. But if being moved by another is a body's trait, moving another is even more so. And the soul moves the body; its impulses show themselves outwardly. It's from the soul that feet are driven to walk, hands to touch, eyes to see, tongue to speak—as a seal impresses a surface by a motion working from inside. Where does an incorporeal soul get this force? How does a void shove solid things?

But how, they ask, do senses split in us into bodily and intellectual? Bodily qualities—earth, fire—are reported by bodily senses: touch, sight. Incorporeal qualities—kindness, malice—belong to intellectual senses. Therefore, they conclude, the soul is incorporeal, since its qualities are grasped not by bodily but by intellectual senses. That is, if I haven't already knocked out that step of the definition. Watch: I show incorporeal things submitting to bodily senses—sound to hearing, color to sight, odor to smell. By that same pattern the soul, too, approaches the body; don't claim it's reported by bodily senses just because it draws near bodily things. So if incorporeal things can be grasped by bodily ones, why can't a bodily soul be reported by incorporeal ones? The definition is sunk.

Another flagship argument: every body is judged by bodily things; the soul, as incorporeal, by incorporeal ones—namely, the pursuit of wisdom. But this rung won't hold either. Even Soranus, the most accomplished author of methodical medicine, answers that the soul is also fed by bodily things; in fact, when it's failing, it's usually propped up by food. Take the food away and it slips out of the body altogether. Soranus himself, after commenting on the soul in four volumes and testing every philosopher's opinion, defends the soul's corporeal substance—though he cheats it of immortality. Not everyone believes what Christians believe. So just as Soranus demonstrates the soul is nourished by bodily things, let the philosopher demonstrate it's fed by incorporeal ones. No one has ever poured honeyed water from Plato's discourse into a hesitating soul, or sprinkled dust from Aristotle's minutiae. What will all those countless souls of peasants and barbarians do—who lack wisdom's nourishment yet thrive on untaught prudence, with no academies, no Attic porticoes, no Socratic prisons, fasting from philosophy, and still live? It's not the substance's nourishment that advances learning, but the disciplines; they don't make the soul richer, only more polished.

And well done: the Stoics, too, declare the arts are bodily. So the soul is bodily as well, if it's thought to be fed by the arts. But philosophy's huge ambition usually can't see past its own feet—like Thales falling down a well. It also suspects sickness when it fails to understand opinions—like Chrysippus turning to hellebore. Something like that, I suspect, happened when it denied two bodies can occupy one space, having lost sight and memory of pregnant women, who don't just carry single bodies day by day but two or three within one womb. Roman law even records a Greek woman bearing five children at once—once mother of all, parent of a single fetus, mother of many, packed with so many bodies she was practically a people, herself the sixth body. The whole order of nature testifies: bodies come from bodies, right there where they originate. What comes from another must be second; nothing comes from another except in being born—and then there are two.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the complex philosophical arguments regarding the soul's movement, its relationship to corporeal and intellectual senses, and the refutation of Platonic definitions. The distinction between 'substance' and 'discipline' is preserved. The translation of the biological/legal example at the end is faithful to the Latin. No scripture was cited in the source, so no errors in citation were possible.
